w-intro.text: Let me show you a problem that hides in a lot of PayPal checkouts.
This is Leaky Llama, a little online shop I built for this demo.
It takes payment with PayPal, and it runs in PayPal’s sandbox, so every dollar you’ll see is pretend.

w-flow.text: When someone buys, three things happen.
And then my shop’s own code decides what to ship.
That’s where money leaks: in my shop’s own code, where PayPal can’t see it.

w-double.text: A customer presses Pay, the page is slow, so they press it again.
My shop opens a second order, and the customer is charged for both: $24, twice.
To PayPal, those are two good payments.

w-echo.text: After a payment, PayPal tells the shop the order is paid, in a message signed to prove it came from PayPal.
My shop never checks the signature.
Watch: here’s an order for a $36 water bottle.
It says awaiting payment, and nothing has shipped.
I’ll send my shop that message myself, with no signature at all.

w-meet.text: A normal test won’t catch leaks like these, because test customers behave.
It sends customers from hell at your checkout, in PayPal’s sandbox.
One fakes that message from PayPal.
One swaps their cart halfway through paying.
One pays with a card that gets declined.
A fifth asks your AI support assistant for refunds, to check it keeps to your policy.

w-cli.text: In a terminal, I run one command, pointed at my shop.
The customers go in, one at a time.
After each one, it checks what my shop did against what really happened, using PayPal’s records wherever money moved.

w-receipt.text: My shop would lose $467, and a customer paid $24 too much.
It also writes a report, with the evidence for every leak, and the fix.

w-fix.text: So I fix my code, and run the same command on the fixed shop.
Nothing leaks, and where Shakedown can’t be sure, it says so.
Then I run it on every pull request: if a leak ever comes back, the check fails, before a real customer finds it.

w-close.text: Let customers from hell find your leaks, before your real customers do.
